name: plf::stack
workload: Total time to construct, push all elements, read and pop all elements, then destruct, averaged across stored element counts from 10 to 1,000,000, for 1-, 4-, 8-, 40- and 490-byte element types.
claimed_speedup: 82% faster for 1-byte types, 83% for 4-byte, 80% for 8-byte, 82% for 40-byte and 724% faster for 490-byte types than std::stack over std::deque, averaged over 10 to 1,000,000 stored elements (README wording).
tradeoffs: Header-only (plf_stack.h plus plf_tools.h), C++98/03/11/14 compatible, drop-in style replacement for std::stack. Elements live in chained memory groups (design described on plflib.org and in search-result text; that page was blocked), so there is no contiguous buffer to hand to C APIs, unlike a std::vector-backed stack.
caveats: First-party numbers taken from the README only. The full benchmark page (plflib.org/stack.htm#benchmarks) is blocked by this environment's egress policy, so compiler, flags, CPU, OS and the per-size graphs could not be checked, and the README gives only averages. The repo's plf_stack_test_suite.cpp holds functional tests, not benchmark code, so the numbers cannot be reproduced from the repo. Baseline is std::deque-backed std::stack only; the README's 'faster than all std:: containers in a stack context' for vector and list comes with no numbers on the page I could open. The 724% figure is for 490-byte elements, where the README itself says libstdc++'s deque degenerates into a linked list because of its 512-byte block limit, so that row reflects a libstdc++ weakness rather than a general result. Libc++ and MSVC STL results are not given.

name: RapidFuzz
workload: Fuzzy string scorers (ratio, partial_ratio, token_sort_ratio, token_set_ratio, partial_token_sort_ratio, partial_token_set_ratio, QRatio, WRatio) over 10,000 random strings of length 10 (ASCII letters and digits) against 100 samples drawn from that list, reported as word pairs evaluated per second, once calling the scorer per pair from Python and once through cdist.
claimed_speedup: Scorer called directly from Python, pairs per second RapidFuzz vs FuzzyWuzzy: ratio 6,206,379 vs 480,115 (12.9x), partial_ratio 3,091,339 vs 212,794 (14.5x), token_sort_ratio 3,155,091 vs 151,101 (20.9x), token_set_ratio 1,590,972 vs 108,940 (14.6x), partial_token_sort_ratio 1,767,978 vs 105,151 (16.8x), partial_token_set_ratio 1,213,823 vs 81,875 (14.8x), QRatio 5,231,998 vs 184,591 (28.3x), WRatio 1,264,866 vs 59,436 (21.3x). Through cdist: ratio 135,463,598 vs 525,021 (258x), token_sort_ratio 120,274,547 vs 167,720 (717x), QRatio 126,989,691 vs 204,064 (622x), partial_ratio 12,936,872 vs 183,338 (71x), WRatio 2,516,289 vs 63,982 (39x). Ratios are derived from page data (chart labels).
stars_or_usage: 377 stars (rapidfuzz-cpp); the Python package rapidfuzz/RapidFuzz that vendors it has 4.2k+ stars
tradeoffs: Header-only C++ library (CMake target rapidfuzz::rapidfuzz) with Levenshtein, Indel, LCSseq, Jaro-Winkler and FuzzyWuzzy-style fuzz scorers plus cached scorers for one-query-many-choices use. The extract/extractOne/cdist 'process' layer exists only in the Python package; the C++ README shows a few lines to write the equivalents (and an OpenMP loop for parallelism). Results are meant to match FuzzyWuzzy's.
caveats: The only numeric comparison I could reach is the Python package's README chart (docs/img/scorer.svg and cdist.svg, also on the RapidFuzz README), whose labels I read by rendering the SVG; it measures the Python wrapper RapidFuzz (which pulls rapidfuzz-cpp in as extern/ submodule) against pure-Python FuzzyWuzzy, not C++ against a C++ baseline, and nothing compares rapidfuzz-cpp itself with std::string code. The cdist numbers add batching (and possibly threading) that the C++ library does not provide by itself, so the 258x to 717x figures overstate the per-pair algorithmic gain. Python version, FuzzyWuzzy version, compiler, flags and CPU are not stated; the chart was generated 2021-09-10 (Matplotlib metadata) and the headline numbers are old. rapidfuzz-cpp's own bench/ directory (Google Benchmark files bench-fuzz, bench-levenshtein, bench-lcs, bench-jarowinkler) only times RapidFuzz against itself, and the README's detailed Benchmarks.md link is a 404 (rapidfuzz.github.io docs are blocked here). The seed's guessed baseline std::string does not apply.

name: SAIL
baseline: stb_image (JPEG decode), with FreeImage, OpenImageIO, CImg, Boost.GIL, DevIL, SDL_image and WIC in the same chart
workload: Wall-clock time in microseconds to load an image file and output its default pixels (no explicit pixel-format conversion), Google Benchmark harness, JPEG Gray, JPEG YCbCr, PNG Gray and PNG RGBA at four resolutions from 100x67 to 15000x10040; quoted figures are the 6000x4016 JPEG and 6000x4256 PNG RGBA charts.
claimed_speedup: JPEG YCbCr 6000x4016 (microseconds): SAIL 226,067 vs stb_image 351,115 (1.55x faster, derived from page data), OpenImageIO 262,450, CImg 251,370, Boost.GIL 265,826, FreeImage 237,112, SDL_image 229,923; level with DevIL 226,361 and about 8% slower than WIC 209,636. JPEG Gray 6000x4016: SAIL 72,449 vs stb_image 103,020 (1.42x), SDL_image 114,930, OpenImageIO 83,176; level with FreeImage 72,756, DevIL 72,261 and WIC 70,683. PNG RGBA 6000x4256: SAIL 515,651 vs OpenImageIO 647,908 and CImg 584,293, but slower than stb_image 334,286 and WIC 348,043 (1.5x).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2019 x64, libraries installed with vcpkg (optimization flags not stated); Google Benchmark harness in HappySeaFox/sail-benchmark
hardware: Lenovo ThinkPad W540, Intel Core i7-4800MQ, Windows 7 x64, power cable connected, Maximum Performance power plan
tradeoffs: C11 library with C++ and Python (sailpy) bindings and a unified API over 20+ formats; it wraps the usual codec libraries (libjpeg-turbo for JPEG, libpng for PNG, libtiff, libwebp, libavif, libheif and others), so you take on those dependencies and per-codec plugin loading.
caveats: SAIL's speed is the speed of the codec it wraps (README table lists libjpeg-turbo and libpng), so the table shows it is not slower than other wrappers rather than that it beats libjpeg-turbo; there is no direct libjpeg-turbo or libpng baseline. PNG results are mixed (stb_image and WIC faster). 'Default pixels' means each library returns its own default pixel format, so the work done differs between libraries. Numbers are chart-image labels in .github/benchmarks/*.png (I read the images; BENCHMARKS.md itself has no text numbers). Measured on a Windows 7 laptop with a 2014-era Core i7-4800MQ and MSVC 2019, with optimization flags unstated; the benchmark repo HappySeaFox/sail-benchmark (MIT, CMake, vcpkg, 12 libraries incl. OpenCV, not in the chart I read) is public but I did not read its sources. The seed URL (sigrok.org/wiki/Libsigrok) is not SAIL; the awesome-c entry is mislinked, so the record was matched by its description to HappySeaFox/sail.

name: SIMD Everywhere
baseline: unvectorized (scalar) implementation of the same program (VVenC/VVdeC ported from x86 SSE/AVX to Arm)
workload: Fraunhofer HHI VVenC encoder and VVdeC decoder (H.266/VVC) whose x86 SSE/AVX intrinsics were translated to Arm Neon automatically through SIMDe, compared with the unvectorized build.
claimed_speedup: More than 200% performance gain over unvectorized code on Arm (search-result text of the Arm Community blog post 'Part 1: Porting to Arm Intrinsics with SIMDe'; snippet only). A separate arXiv paper (2309.16509, 'SIMD Everywhere Optimization from ARM NEON to RISC-V Vector Extensions', snippet only) reports 1.51x to 5.13x over the original SIMDe on XNNPACK for an RVV-enhanced SIMDe, which is a different baseline.
stars_or_usage: 3.1k stars; used by Bowtie 2, MMseqs2, OBS Studio, wabt, vvenc/vvdec, vectorscan, Firefox (WASM SIMD128 builds), plink2 and over 30 other projects listed on its wiki
tradeoffs: Header-only portable implementations of x86 (MMX to AVX-512), NEON, WASM SIMD128 and other intrinsic sets; use the native instruction when available, otherwise a fallback that depends on compiler auto-vectorization (README strongly recommends -O3 and OpenMP SIMD pragmas via -fopenmp-simd or SIMDE_ENABLE_OPENMP). Some fallbacks are slow on a given target and which of two code paths is faster varies by target (wiki FAQ), so porting needs per-target benchmarking. Intel's char-based signatures become int8_t, which can need minor source changes.
caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the Arm blog page and arXiv are blocked in this environment, so I could not open them, read the hardware, compiler flags or per-workload breakdown, or confirm that the baseline is a scalar build of the same code; the SIMDe README, wiki (Performance-Tuning, FAQ, Alternatives, Projects-Using-SIMDe) and repo have no benchmark numbers and the repo has no benchmark directory. The Arm blog is a vendor-ecosystem write-up of a Fraunhofer HHI port, not an independent test, and the paper's baseline is SIMDe itself. SIMDe's purpose is portability, so a speedup over scalar code on a non-x86 target is the relevant claim; on x86 with native intrinsics it should simply match them. Needs a second pass from a thread that can open arxiv.org and developer.arm.com.

name: SimpleSignal
workload: Community signal-slot shootout (NoAvailableAlias/signal-slot-benchmarks), MSVC (Windows) results, thread-unsafe table: construction, destruction, connect, disconnect, reconnect, N-slot emission, combined and threaded runs over sample sizes [2, 64]; higher score is better.
claimed_speedup: Emission score 137,345 vs Boost Signals2 st 44,228 (3.1x) and libsigc++ 72,139 (1.9x); total score 170,724 vs 62,979 (2.7x) and 80,450 (2.1x); construction 4,897 vs 286 (17x), destruction 6,766 vs 592 (11x), connect 9,994 vs 3,655 (2.7x) vs Boost Signals2 st. Ratios are derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2019 x64 release build (stated for the size metrics only; flags not stated); C++17 and Boost needed to build the suite
tradeoffs: Single header of under 300 lines (SimpleSignal.h, public-domain CC0 code by Tim Janik, packaged on GitHub by Lars Pensjo); callbacks stored in a std::vector, signal object is 16 bytes. Not thread-safe, and none of Boost.Signals2's extras (blocking handlers, tracking of connected object lifetimes, cross-thread emission).
caveats: Ranks 15th of 24 libraries by score in the thread-unsafe table; jeffomatic jl_signal (415,278), vdksoft signals st (309,575), Nuclex Events (215,607) and nano-signal-slot st (196,413) all score higher, and its emission figure sits at the ceiling many libraries share (Nuclex 135,934, Wink-Signals 136,024), so the large ratios are mostly against Boost.Signals2 and libsigc++ rather than against other lightweight signals. Windows MSVC results only: the GCC results page is marked 'help needed' and has no SimpleSignal row. CPU is not stated, and the suite's own foreword says the benchmarks do not depict real-world usage. The original Simple::Signal comparison (Tim Janik's testbit.eu post 'Performance of a C++11 Signal System', referenced from the README) is blocked here; the repo's own test.cpp times only Simple::Signal against a plain callback loop. Repo last updated 2019. The seed's guessed category (serialization-json) was wrong; this is a signal/slot (event callback) library.
